1.title: Developer Productivity and Operational Enablement
1.text: Welcome to Module seventeen: Developer Productivity and Operational Enablement. This module covers developer productivity and operational enablement. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do four things. How to configure Claude Code for a team: scopes, shared settings, managed policy. Team standards: Claude dot M D, permissions, hooks, Skills, plugins, M C P (Model Context Protocol). A I-assisted workflows and their guardrails. Operational enablement: debugging, incidents, cost and usage visibility.

1.title: Case Check-In: Lumen Advisory Rolls Out Claude Code to a Bank's 300 Engineers
1.text: Our running case is Lumen Advisory. Lumen Advisory Rolls Out Claude Code to a Bank's three hundred Engineers. The bank's security team wants model and permission limits and no secrets exposure. Platform engineering wants shared standards and usage visibility by team. Developers want autonomy in their own folders.

1.title: Configuring Claude Code for Teams
1.text: Configuring Claude Code for Teams. Four settings scopes. User. File: about or dot Claude settings.json. Applies to: One developer, all projects. Use for: Personal preferences. Shared project. File: dot Claude settings.json (commit it). Applies to: Everyone in the repository. Use for: Team permissions, hooks, plugins, project environment variables. Project local. File: dot Claude settings.local.json (kept out of git). Applies to: One developer, one project. Use for: Personal overrides. Managed. File: Deployed by the organization (managed-settings.json, M D M, or server-managed settings from the admin console). Applies to: Everyone it is deployed to. Use for: Security policy and compliance.

1.title: Configuring Claude Code for Teams, continued
1.text: Configuring Claude Code for Teams, continued. The figure shows this: Settings precedence from highest to lowest: managed, command line, project local, shared project, user; list settings such as permission rules merge across scopes. Precedence (highest first): managed, command line, project local, shared project, user. A key set higher overrides the same key below it; lists such as permission rules merge across scopes.

1.title: Configuring Claude Code for Teams, continued
1.text: Configuring Claude Code for Teams, continued. Managed settings lock what developers cannot change: allowed and denied models (available Models, denied Models), permission policy, telemetry destination, and more. A few restrictive keys are honored from any scope. Repository files cannot grant everything: for example bypass Permissions and telemetry exporters do not take effect from project settings, and committed allow rules wait for the developer to trust the folder. Verify with or status (which sources loaded) and claude doctor (rejected entries). Exam tip: To enforce a policy developers must not override, use managed settings. To share team conventions, commit dot Claude settings.json and Claude dot M D. Personal tweaks belong in user or local files.

1.title: Team Standards and Extensions
1.text: Team Standards and Extensions. Claude dot M D (committed). Purpose: Persistent project instructions: conventions, commands, architecture notes. Notes: Keep concise; it loads into context. Permission rules (allow, ask, deny). Purpose: What Claude may run or read. Notes: Deny secrets files (for example.env) and dangerous commands. Hooks. Purpose: Deterministic scripts at events (for example before a tool runs). Notes: Enforce rules prompts cannot guarantee: block, format, log. Skills. Purpose: Reusable procedures loaded on demand. Notes: Share review checklists, migration procedures. Plugins. Purpose: Bundle skills, commands, hooks and M C P servers for distribution. Notes: Record sources and versions. M C P servers (shared config). Purpose: Connect issue trackers, docs, databases. Notes: Apply least privilege and OAuth (Module eight).

1.title: Team Standards and Extensions, continued
1.text: Team Standards and Extensions, continued. Sandboxing. Purpose: Contain commands and file access. Notes: Reduce blast radius. Headless mode (claude dash p). Purpose: Run in scripts and C I. Notes: Use scoped permissions; dash dash bare skips auto-discovery for reproducible scripted runs. Secrets: never in Claude dot M D or committed settings; deny reads of secret files; use environment variables and a secrets manager. Model and cost control: restrict available models by policy; use Open Telemetry to see cost and tokens by team.

1.title: Team Standards and Extensions, continued
1.text: Team Standards and Extensions, continued. Telemetry is off until enabled; metrics include cost, token usage by type, sessions, commits, pull requests and tool decisions; prompt content is not logged by default; admins push settings through managed settings; add team and cost-center attributes with O T E L R E S O U R C E A T T R I B U T E S (watch label cardinality). Exam tip: Managed settings enforce what developers must not override; committed Claude dot M D and dot Claude settings.json share conventions. Exam tip: Hooks and permission rules enforce deterministically; a sentence in Claude dot M D is only guidance.

1.title: AI-Assisted Developer Workflows
1.text: A I-Assisted Developer Workflows. The figure shows this: A I-assisted development loop: plan, implement with Claude, verify with tests and human review, merge, and capture lessons in Claude dot M D and skills.

1.title: AI-Assisted Developer Workflows, continued
1.text: A I-Assisted Developer Workflows, continued. Code understanding. How Claude helps: Explore a large codebase, explain modules. Guardrail: Verify claims against the code. Implementation. How Claude helps: Plan, then implement changes across files. Guardrail: Plan mode first; small reviewed diffs. Tests. How Claude helps: Generate and extend tests; run them. Guardrail: Tests are the verification; review test quality. Code review. How Claude helps: First-pass review in C I against team rules. Guardrail: Human reviewers remain accountable. Documentation. How Claude helps: Draft and update docs. Guardrail: Review for accuracy. Migrations and refactors. How Claude helps: Repetitive edits at scale. Guardrail: Scripted checks, staged rollout. Verification over trust: run tests, linters and type checks; require review; do not merge unreviewed A I changes.

1.title: AI-Assisted Developer Workflows, continued
1.text: A I-Assisted Developer Workflows, continued. Plan first for non-trivial work; keep changes small. Capture lessons in Claude dot M D and Skills so the next session starts better. Measure productivity honestly (cycle time, review time, defect rate), not only lines produced. Protect I P and data: control what code and data may leave the environment; use managed policy and approved platforms.

1.title: Debugging and Operational Support
1.text: Debugging and Operational Support. Incident triage: Claude can read logs, traces and recent changes, form hypotheses and propose fixes; keep read-only access by default and approval for production changes. Reproduce first: use request ids, trace ids, prompt and model versions to replay (Module twelve). Runbooks as Skills: encode diagnosis procedures so responders and Claude follow the same steps. Observability access: connect monitoring and ticket systems through M C P with least privilege. Post-incident: update runbooks, evals and Claude dot M D with the lesson. Usage visibility: dashboards of cost and tokens by team, budgets and alerts; Claude Code analytics and usage A P I s (application programming interface) report per-user estimates for governance.

1.title: Module Recap
1.text: Here is the recap. Scopes: User, shared project (commit), project local (not committed), managed (org). Precedence: Managed greater than command line greater than project local greater than shared project greater than user; lists merge. Policy: Managed settings (models, permissions, telemetry); or status, claude doctor. Standards: Claude dot M D, permission rules, hooks, Skills, plugins, M C P, sandbox. Deterministic: Hooks and permission rules, not prose. Telemetry: Off until enabled; no prompt text by default; managed settings; team attributes. Workflows: Plan, small diffs, tests, review, capture lessons. Ops: Read-only by default; approval for prod changes; runbooks as Skills.

1.title: Practice Question 1
1.text: Question one. A security team must ensure developers cannot use unapproved models or bypass permission policy. Which mechanism enforces this? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Managed settings sit at the top of precedence and cannot be overridden.

1.title: Practice Question 2
1.text: Question two. Where should team conventions such as build commands and architecture notes be stored so every developer's sessions use them? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Committed, shared files give everyone the same standards.

1.title: Practice Question 3
1.text: Question three. A developer sets model in project local settings; a managed setting restricts allowed models. What happens? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Managed policy has the highest precedence, so a project-local value cannot override an organization's model restriction.

1.title: Practice Question 4
1.text: Question four. Select two. Which two enforce behavior deterministically rather than by instruction? The five options are on the screen. The answers are A and C. Hooks and permission rules are enforced by the tool, not by the model's compliance.

1.title: Practice Question 5
1.text: Question five. The platform team wants cost and token usage by team from Claude Code. What should they do? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Telemetry through managed settings gives cost data; prompt content stays off by default.

1.title: Practice Question 6
1.text: Question six. A repository's committed settings try to configure the telemetry exporter and bypass Permissions. What is the result? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Security-sensitive keys such as bypass Permissions and telemetry exporters are ignored from repository files and need managed or user settings.

1.title: Practice Question 7
1.text: Question seven. An A I-generated change passes review quickly but later breaks production. Which workflow improvement is most relevant? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B. Verification and accountable human review remain essential: plan first, keep diffs small, run tests and review meaningfully.

1.title: Practice Question 8
1.text: Question eight. During an incident, an assistant should help diagnose a production fault. What access design is appropriate? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C. Read-only access by default with approval for production changes follows least privilege during incident response.

1.title: Practice Question 9
1.text: Question nine. A team wants a reusable diagnosis procedure that both responders and Claude follow. What fits best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D. A shared Skill packages the runbook as a procedure that loads when the situation matches, so responders and Claude follow the same steps.

1.title: Practice Question 10
1.text: Question ten. Why is Claude Code telemetry not logging prompt text by default? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A. Content gates are off by default and must be enabled deliberately.

1.title: Answers at a Glance
1.text: Here are all ten answers. Question one: A. Question two: B. Question three: C. Question four: A and C. Question five: B. Question six: B. Question seven: B. Question eight: C. Question nine: D. Question ten: A. In the next module, we continue the course.
